source.title: How Far Do Auto-Interpretation Labels Generalize: A Controlled Study Across Languages, Scripts, and Rewordings

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether SAE features and their labels generalize across equivalent language and script forms; the results refine the claim that dictionary features are stable, complete units, showing feature-level misses that vary by form and depth.
record.gate_note: The study does not test toy-model superposition, overcomplete geometric directions, or capacity competition. It does measure SAE active-feature-set overlap and auto-interpretation-label miss rates on controlled equivalent inputs. Reported classifier discard rates, tokenization analyses, validation statistics, and cited findings are not rows because they do not measure the claim versions directly.
record.test_reason: The study uses public Gemma Scope SAEs on Gemma-3 models to test two things: whether same-meaning inputs activate overlapping SAE features beyond a random baseline (Leg 1), and whether content features fire consistently on equivalent renderings (Leg 2). Leg 1 bears weakly on V4: SAEs recover sparse, meaning-tracking features. Leg 2 bears on V5 only in a narrow sense, namely invariance of a feature across input forms. It does not address completeness, stability across training seeds, or canonicality across dictionary sizes. The paper's aim is auto-interpretation label reliability, not superposition.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that SAE features encode abstract cross-lingual meaning, but content labels fail on less-represented forms. Misses run up to 4x the within-language floor for Serbian and up to 1.35x for Cyrillic vs Latin. The failure is graded by estimated training coverage, sharpens with depth, and is invisible from the label. Labels should be read as claims about a feature's best-represented inputs.
record.recipe_differences: Measures multilingual active-feature-set overlap and tests auto-interpretation-label miss rates using controlled translated, transliterated, and paraphrased inputs; it does not reproduce toy-network superposition geometry or its sparsity/importance interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Miss rates and Serbian Cyrillic/Latin asymmetry vary with layer depth; the Cyrillic disadvantage is small or statistically indistinguishable from parity in early layers and larger at later layers. Labeler choice changes which features are classified as content claims, but the paper reports a similar asymmetry for Claude Sonnet and Gemini. Feature-set overlap decomposition is reported as robust to SAE sparsity, dictionary width, pooling choice, Gemma scale, and a Llama model, with effect-size differences across setups.
record.problems: The main evaluation uses 300 sentences and three languages, with Serbian closely related to Russian. Leg 2 is reported for Gemma scales but not verified across other model families or labeling pipelines. A single annotator manually inspected missed features, and the authors note that another related feature may fire when a tested feature does not. The exact layer-wise confidence intervals for Figure 1 are not stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted to meet the row limit. The paper also reports additional labeler, paraphrase-condition, topic-bucket, and scale-specific miss-rate breakdowns; only the main 27B layer-wise results, key controls, and deepest reported 1B/12B replication results are tabulated here.

untested.parts: All of it: toy networks, overlapping near-orthogonal directions, sparsity-dependent phase transitions, geometry.
All of it: neuron polysemanticity and capacity competition.
All of it: no neuron-level polysemanticity analysis.
Whether features are spread across many neurons; no neuron-basis analysis. Only SAE feature-set overlap is measured.
Completeness, stability across SAE seeds or training runs, and canonicality across dictionary sizes. Whether other features fire in place of missed ones is not examined (authors' limitation).
All of it: no test of feature dimensionality.

missing.what: Leg 1 meaning-overlap replications on Gemma-3-1B and 12B, and on Llama-3.1-8B with Llama Scope 32k SAEs. Meaning stays above baseline in all; Llama absolute Jaccard is lower (script 0.48 vs 0.73).
Leg 1 robustness to SAE width (262k vs 16k) and L0 sparsity: the ordering is preserved, with a uniform downward shift at 262k width.

Human check of 60 missed units. Labels match their top examples in 92% (Yes+Partly), but the labeled concept is present in the missed sentence in only 58%. Features are driven by more than their labels.
Gemini-labeled 27B miss rates and Cyr/Lat ratios (1.03–1.36), plus Serbian paraphrase miss rates.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not aimed at superposition. The V5 link rests on reading 'stable/canonical units' as including invariance across equivalent inputs. The authors attribute the misses to the features rather than the labelers, but note that a related feature may fire instead. The selection anchors (English original, Russian paraphrase) make cross-language miss magnitudes upper bounds; the Cyr/Lat ratio is unaffected. Single model family for Leg 2; 300 sentences.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks with more sparse features than dimensions; overlapping nearly orthogonal directions; sparsity-dependent transitions and regular geometry.
Neuron polysemanticity, limited representational capacity, dedicated dimensions for important features, and competition or sharing.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure or whether they evidence superposition.
The study tests SAE feature-set overlap in language models, but does not measure features spread across neurons or establish a complete feature dictionary.

Tests cross-form consistency of active SAE features and their labels, but does not establish that SAE features are complete or canonical units, or whether other features compensate when a tested feature fails to fire.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.subject: Gemma-3-27B
rows.operation_detail: Compared active SAE feature sets for the same Serbian sentence in Cyrillic and Latin; mean Jaccard overlap across layers.
rows.measure: Mean Jaccard similarity of active feature sets
rows.uncertainty: 95% bootstrap confidence bands shown; exact interval not stated
rows.note: The authors describe this as preserving most of the active set and as the mildest of the four tested perturbations.
rows.check: This is a surface-property control (script only). It isolates the effect of script on the active set and does not measure whether recoverable sparse features exist, so it does not bear on V4.

rows.subject: Gemma-3-27B
rows.operation_detail: Compared active SAE feature sets for the same content in Serbian and Russian, both Cyrillic.
rows.measure: Mean Jaccard similarity of active feature sets
rows.uncertainty: 95% bootstrap confidence bands shown; exact interval not stated
rows.note: The study reports less overlap than for the Serbian script comparison.
rows.check: This is a language control (Sr vs Ru, same script), not a test of V4. 'Partial' has no meaning relative to V4.

rows.subject: Gemma-3-27B
rows.operation_detail: Compared active SAE feature sets for an English sentence and its English paraphrase.
rows.measure: Mean Jaccard similarity of active feature sets
rows.uncertainty: 95% bootstrap confidence bands shown; exact interval not stated
rows.note: Substantial active-set overlap remains under rewording, below the identity ceiling.
rows.check: This is a wording control read against the identity ceiling, not a V4 measure.

rows.subject: Gemma-3-27B
rows.operation_detail: Compared active SAE feature sets for the same meaning in English and Russian, with script, language, and wording changed.
rows.measure: Mean Jaccard similarity of active feature sets
rows.uncertainty: 95% bootstrap confidence bands shown; exact interval not stated
rows.note: The authors interpret overlap above the random baseline as evidence that SAE feature sets encode abstract meaning.
rows.check: Link is correct. Mean Jaccard is 0.39 vs random baseline 0.13, peaking at 0.57. This shows SAE features shared by same-meaning inputs, which is indirect V4 evidence. It says nothing about spread across neurons.

relationships.condition: Gemma-3-27B, Gemma Scope 2 16k JumpReLU SAEs, last-token residual stream, 300 FLORES+ sentences
relationships.reason: English original vs Russian paraphrase share SAE features well above the random-partner baseline (0.39 vs 0.13, peak 0.57) (r4). This is indirect evidence that SAEs recover sparse semantic features.
relationships.display_finding: English originals and Russian paraphrases shared SAE features well above the random-partner baseline (0.39 vs 0.13, peak 0.57), indirect evidence that the SAEs recover sparse semantic features.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Gemma-3-27B, Gemma Scope 2 16k JumpReLU SAEs, last-token residual stream, 300 FLORES+ sentences
source_check.reason: r4 reports semantic-pair Jaccard overlap 0.39 versus random-partner 0.13, peaking at 0.57: indirect evidence of recoverable sparse semantic features.

relationships.condition: Gemma-3-27B content-labeled features, layers 31–53, Sonnet-content and unfiltered pools
relationships.reason: Features that fire on English and Russian miss Serbian 20–35% of the time vs 7–17% within-language (r5–r8). They also miss Cyrillic more than its lossless Latin transliteration, with ratios of 1.11–1.35 growing with depth (r10–r12, r18–r20). So individual features are not form-invariant units of a concept.
relationships.display_finding: Features firing on English and Russian missed Serbian 20–35% of the time vs 7–17% within a language, and missed Cyrillic more than its lossless Latin transliteration (ratios 1.11–1.35, growing with depth), so features were not form-invariant units of a concept.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Gemma-3-27B content-labeled features, layers 31–53, Sonnet-content and unfiltered pools
source_check.reason: r6–r8, r10–r12 and r18–r20 show incomplete semantic activation consistency across languages and scripts. This qualifies stable semantic-unit interpretations; completeness and canonical dictionary identity remain untested.

relationships.condition: Gemma-3-12B and Gemma-3-1B, deepest reported layers, Gemini labels
relationships.reason: Serbian miss rates (32.6%, 53.8%) far exceed within-language floors. The Cyr/Lat ratio is 1.33 at 12B; at 1B it is 1.18, with a CI reaching parity (r21–r24).
relationships.display_finding: Serbian miss rates of 32.6% and 53.8% far exceeded within-language floors; the Cyrillic/Latin miss ratio was 1.33 at 12B and 1.18 at 1B, where the confidence interval reached parity.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Gemma-3-12B and Gemma-3-1B, deepest reported layers, Gemini labels
source_check.reason: r21–r24 replicate incomplete cross-language activation consistency. The 12B script-ratio interval excludes parity; the 1B interval reaches parity. These results qualify semantic invariance without testing canonicality.

relation.reason: The study reports controlled semantic-feature overlap and individual-feature activation failures on equivalent renderings.

tranche.reason: The main controlled results show that semantic interpretations of individual SAE features require language- and script-dependent qualifications. This fits T5; the auxiliary overlap analysis supplies new-setting V4 evidence.

source_check.notes: English/Russian anchoring makes absolute cross-language magnitudes upper bounds; the script ratio is unaffected. Appendix D.2 finds the labeled concept present at least partly in only 58% of 60 sampled misses, limiting concept-specific interpretations.

statements.correction: Gemma-3-27B, Sonnet content pool, layer 53: Serbian Latin miss rate 25.6%; Serbian Cyrillic 34.6%; Cyrillic/Latin ratio 1.35. Verdict: limits_scope for form-invariant semantic interpretation; canonicality and cross-seed identity untested.
statements.problem: The numbers and conditions match, but the challenges label overstates these partially generalizing results and conflicts with the condition-specific limits_scope verdict.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Gemma-3-27B active SAE feature-set comparisons on 300 controlled sentences
reader_labels.reason: Same-meaning English and Russian inputs have mean feature-set Jaccard 0.39 versus 0.13 random baseline, with overlap also measured across Serbian scripts and wording (r1–r4). This supports SAE-recoverable semantic feature structure, not the stronger claim that features are spread across neurons.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Gemma-3-27B content-labeled features across tested language/script renderings and layers
reader_labels.reason: Features selected as content-related still fail to fire on equivalent inputs; misses are higher for Serbian and the Cyrillic disadvantage grows with depth, so feature labels or activations are not uniformly stable across forms (r5–r12). The study does not test whether other features compensate.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Gemma-3-27B unfiltered pool and Gemma-3-1B/12B replications
reader_labels.reason: The Serbian script asymmetry persists without the content classifier and is also reported across Gemma scales, though the deepest 1B ratio has an interval reaching parity (r17–r24).
